summary: This final issue of South Korean Interim Government Activities, prepared by the National Economic Board Statistics Division, covers July-August 1948 and the transition on 15 August 1948 from US Army Military Government to the Republic of Korea under President Rhee Syngman. It opens with a summation of three years of occupation, citing food self-sufficiency prospects, fertilizer imports, farmland sales, a narrowing trade deficit and vested property returned to Korean management. Regular sections report prices (wholesale index 184 percent of 1947), industrial output under reduced power after the 14 May North Korean cutoff, labor, transport, communications, finance with a 22,000 million won overdraft, politics, police, and social fields. Historians will find refugee and population statistics, trade figures, the Constitution and cabinet formation, and retrospective accounts of each department.
highlights: Republic of Korea proclaimed 15 August 1948; USAMGIK succeeded by Civil Affairs Section of USAFIK.
Refugees from north: 185,441 in 1946, 163,235 in 1947, 86,036 by mid-August 1948.
Wholesale prices rose to 184 percent of the 1947 average in August.
SKIG overdraft exceeded 22,000 million won at the end of August.
Local power generation reached 55,600,000 KWH in August versus 33,000,000 in April.
Management of 35 vested companies transferred to elected Boards of Directors; 481,957 acres of farmland sold.
Korea competed in the London Olympics under its own flag for the first time.
Torture death case in Metropolitan Police and attack on Chief Chang reported.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover and front matter of the final SKIG Activities report (No. 34, July-August 1948), prepared by the National Economic Board. Lists Board members under Chairman Wilhelm Anderson and Statistics Division contributors. Arthur G. Peterson's Forward records the 15 August 1948 founding of the Republic, the report's lineage since 1946, poor Korean statistics, and staff losses. Includes the full table of contents.

sections.title: Summary
sections.summary: Chairman Wilhelm Anderson reviews three years of occupation as the Republic was proclaimed on 15 August 1948. Cites refugee and repatriate inflows, 500,000 tons of imported fertilizer, near food self-sufficiency, the narrowing trade gap, the power cutoff of 14 May, 85,000 million won of vested property, 481,957 acres of farmland sold, inflation, and a 22,000 million won overdraft.

sections.title: Part I: Basic Aspects
sections.summary: Population and foreign affairs, and vested property.

sections.title: Section 1. Population and Foreign Affairs
sections.summary: Covers refugees, repatriation and population statistics. Refugees from the north totalled 86,036 in 1948 to mid-August, after 185,441 in 1946; cumulative inbound movement was 2,454,480 against 886,618 outbound, mostly Japanese. 151 stateless Turk-Tartars awaited emigration to Turkey. Demographic estimates give 3.1 percent natural increase, a population of 20.3 million, and the Population and Census Committee's projections.

sections.title: Section 2. Vested Property
sections.summary: Office of Property Custody prepares for handover to the Republic, reorganizing its Administration Division and inspecting textile and paper plants. Disposal sales and the return of Army-occupied property reached new highs. Claims hearings on title disputes covered 1,119 cases nationwide, and a policy memorandum released Allied-owned property. Corporate Affairs investigated 5,358 companies; 35 passed to elected boards. Net worth of vested property totalled about 85,850 million won.

sections.title: Part II: Production and Supply
sections.summary: Agriculture, prices, industry, mining, distribution, trade, labor.

sections.title: Section 1. Food and Agriculture
sections.summary: South Korea's 1948 crop is estimated near 6,000,000 metric tons, the highest since 1941, with food self-sufficiency expected by January 1949. Summer grain collection reached 95.8 percent of quota. The 7 July typhoon and floods damaged Cholla coastal levees. Fertilizer imports passed 548,000 tons and Korea Agricultural Association took over distribution. National Land Administration had sold 481,957 acres, covering 85 percent of available farms.

sections.title: Section 2. Prices
sections.summary: Wholesale prices rose to 184 percent of the 1947 average in August, from 171 in July, ending five months of stability, led by grains, fish, raw cotton and salt. Controlled prices for rice, barley and wheat rose on 1 August and for salt on 15 August. Seoul retail prices roughly doubled for grains over August 1947. A new weighted urban worker index stood at 179 in August.

sections.title: Section 3. Industrial Production
sections.summary: Explains why 1947 South Korean output looks far below 1940 (incomplete reporting, home production of noodles and cloth), then reports July-August 1948 under the power shortage: flour 707 and 1,782 tons, paper mills short of pulp, cement halted, rubber shoes steady, salt hit by rains, and Monopoly Bureau tobacco revenue and cigarette paper problems.

sections.title: Section 4. Mining and Minerals
sections.summary: Coal output fell after the Soviets cut North Korean power on 14 May 1948: anthracite dropped from 68,612 tons in April to 38,887 in July, and Hwasun was flooded. Bituminous imports from Japan reached a record 104,055 tons in July. Covers August allocations, coal pitch stockpiling, Yong Wol, and gold, copper, tungsten, graphite, zinc and lead output.

sections.title: Section 5. Allocations and Distribution
sections.summary: Describes the National Consumer Goods Office (est. 12 January 1948), which processed 1,095 allocations worth 2.18 billion won by 31 August, and the Federation of Financial Associations distributing goods to about 480,000 eligible employees. Also covers petroleum deliveries, salt supply for F/Y 1947-1949 (68,774 tons produced by 15 August), and barter with North Korea (950.9 million won inflow).

sections.title: Section 6. Imports and Exports
sections.summary: Private trade totaled about 3,643 million won in imports and 2,763 million in exports for January-July 1948, with paper the leading import and sea products and straw hats leading exports. Covers licensing rules, the Trustee Shipment plan, ship movements, government exports to Japan ($828,457), the US and Hong Kong, PX sales, and Civilian Supply imports (FLC, coal, food, salt, fertilizer, petroleum).

sections.title: Section 7. Labor
sections.summary: Surveys three years of labor: about 118,000 unionists in some 500 unions, mostly in rightist Tai Han, with Chun Pyung underground. Reviews labor laws, the NEB's wage policy and the Wage Stabilization Division (25 March 1948). July-August items: Pusan stevedore wage talks (350 won minimum), Yongwol election won by Tai Han (2,099 votes), Tai Han executive resignation, bank overtime violations and a labor education tour.

sections.title: Part III: Public Services
sections.summary: Transportation, communications, public utilities and public works.

sections.title: Section 1. Transportation
sections.summary: Reviews the Department of Transportation since 1945: Japanese departure, shortages of parts and coal, and expenditures exceeding income. August revenue was the highest since liberation. Rail section gives 268 operable engines in August, higher freight income, passenger, tonnage, coal and employment tables. Also covers marine fleet (LSTs, Rainbow service), Japanese-era trucking, floods and rising marine expenditure.

sections.title: Section 2. Communications
sections.summary: Describes the Department of Communications: Japanese-era organization, wartime neglect and the American rehabilitation of telephone exchanges. July revenue was the highest since liberation (June rate increase), while expenditures more than doubled to 196.9 million won. Covers staff cuts, postal savings and insurance, 37,183 telephones, telegraph declines, 623 post offices and 11 radio stations.

sections.title: Section 3. Public Utilities
sections.summary: Traces electric power from Japanese neglect through 1948. The North Korean shut-off of 14 May 1948 and the Chung Pyung transformer failure caused shortages, but deliveries recovered to 56.2 million KWH in July and 55.6 million in August. Covers plant output, the Yong Wol overhaul directive of 26 July, the Giroux Commission report of 23 July and Seoul and Pusan streetcar and bus service.

sections.title: Section 4. Public Works
sections.summary: Reviews public works since 1910 and under the Military Government: department status in August 1946, Koreanization and lessons learned. Summer 1948 brought preparation for transfer to the Korean Government and flood damage exceeding 2,000 million won. Covers road and bridge repairs and subsidy requests, the Emergency Water Conservation Board of 28 July, and fire statistics for the first half of 1948.

sections.title: Part IV: Finance
sections.summary: Government and non-government finance.

sections.title: Section 1. Government Finance
sections.summary: Reports Bank of Chosun note issue of about 30,000 million won at end of August and an SKIG overdraft of 22,506 million won. Revenues of 2,157 million won in August against expenditures of 1,924 million. Gives fiscal-year revenue and expenditure totals, F/Y 1948/49 appropriations of 35,264 million won including 6,260 million for civilian supply, and civilian supply assets of 38,465 million won.

sections.title: Section 2. Non-Government Finance
sections.summary: Covers private finance through July (August data unavailable). Cash balances were 2,244 million won; deposits reached 43,335 million won, 57 percent held by the public. Loans outstanding were 30,038 million won with record new lending in June and July. Life insurance in force passed 1,067 million won, and damage insurers wrote 9,243 new policies in July.

sections.title: Part V: Government and Politics
sections.summary: Administration, political developments, legal affairs, police, inter-zone activities.

sections.title: Section 1. Administration
sections.summary: The new government (Tai Han Min Kook) was proclaimed 15 August 1948, ending USAMGIK; the 10 May election drew over 90 per cent of 7,730,000 registered voters. The National Economic Board met five times, raising rice to 150 won per small mal and approving fare and per diem increases. Table shows MG personnel falling to 2,870 by 15 August.

sections.title: Section 2. Political Developments
sections.summary: Covers the Constitution (12 July) and Government Organization Law, giving the President strong powers and state control of major industries. The Assembly elected Rhee Syngman President (180 votes) and Lee Si-young Vice-President, approved Lee Bum-suk as Prime Minister 110 to 84, and fought over cabinet picks. Moderates split three ways between Kim Koo, Kimm Kiu-sic and the North.

sections.title: Section 3. Legal Affairs
sections.summary: The Department of Justice drafted Ordinances Nos. 203-219 and Executive Orders Nos. 24-28, covering litigation fees, the bar, rice collection, school districts and narcotics informers. Opinions addressed Japanese repatriate pensions and the Chosun Mining monopoly. Cheju-do riot trials were movable to Mokpo or Kwangju. Prisoners numbered 22,321 in July; 664 juveniles were in correction houses.

sections.title: Section 4. National Police
sections.summary: Police concentrated on communist efforts to force signatures for the 25 August North Korean election, with arrests in Pusan, Chungchong and Cholla provinces and 200 officials held in Taegu. A torture death by Metropolitan Police caused Detective Bureau resignations. Chang Taik-sang became Foreign Minister, and a fourth attempt on his life failed on 24 July.

sections.title: Section 5. Inter-Zone Activities
sections.summary: North-South mail exchange continued at Tosong, with 9 trips in July-August 1948 and tabulated letter counts. Commerce Order No. 4 on overland interzonal barter took effect 2 August, and June imports included 516 tons of fertilizer. An American soldier was killed at the 38th parallel on 19 July. Radio Pyongyang attacked Rhee and promoted the 25 August election.

sections.title: Part VI: Social
sections.summary: Health, education, press, youth, women, culture.

sections.title: Section 1. Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: Floods and typhoons left 254,664 people needy, and hog cholera hit five provinces, with 43,428 hogs affected by mid-August. Two smallpox outbreaks were controlled, with about 420,000 vaccinated in Seoul. Reports cover nurse graduations, narcotics seizures, 28,698 kg of opium returned to Japan, vaccine stocks, tents for refugees, new orphanages and UNRRA grants.

sections.title: Section 2. Education
sections.summary: Three ordinances effective 12 August 1948 created school districts, nine-member school boards and local school taxation. The Department also reported teacher workshops reaching 7,500 teachers, a new elementary achievement test, scholarship screening, textbook output (421,660 copies in July), American Language Institute classes, vocational committees in Pusan, home economics sessions and adult education conferences.

sections.title: Section 3. Press and Public Opinion
sections.summary: The press dwelt on forming the new government: the Constitution, the police-under-Internal Affairs vote (108 to 88), rejection of Lee Yun-yung and approval of Lee Bum-suk as Premier, and attacks on Rhee's cabinet. It also covered the North Korean election, floods, Cheju-do riots, Dok Do compensation, and a table of 11 leading dailies among 58.

sections.title: Section 4. Korean National Youth, Inc.
sections.summary: Describes Korean National Youth, Inc., chartered 9 October 1945 with Military Government backing, as a community-service alternative to terrorist youth groups. Membership reached 1,154,821 by 15 August 1948; members gave over 12,600,000 work-days of labor. Covers training, terror opposition, and the succession of Lee Jun-sic after Lee Bum-suk became Prime Minister.

sections.title: Section 5. Women's Activities
sections.summary: Reports that the new Constitution and Military Government ordinances guarantee women equality, and that women now work in many professions. Notes Mrs. Rhee, Louise Yim as Minister of Commerce and Industry, teachers and students abroad, religious work, and ordinances against selling women. Describes primitive home life and the Women's Bureau's magazine, classes and Federation of Women's Clubs.

sections.title: Section 6. Culture
sections.summary: Covers Hangul's reintroduction in schools, with problems of Chinese characters, orthography and printing, plus the Bible Society shipment and a new dictionary. Describes the American Language Institute's English courses (about 500 students). Reports Korea's first Olympic entry under its own flag at London, 67 athletes, 24th place with 15 points; pages 484-485 are blank.
